questions.question: A Deployment specifies three replicas. One Pod is deleted manually. What normally happens?
options: The Deployment scales down to two replicas
An administrator must recreate the Pod
The deleted Pod restarts with the same UID
The ReplicaSet creates a replacement Pod
questions.explanation: The ReplicaSet reconciles the actual Pod count with the desired count. The replacement Pod has a new UID.

questions.question: Which Service type provides an internal cluster IP by default?
options: ExternalName
ClusterIP
LoadBalancer
NodePort
questions.explanation: ClusterIP is the default Service type. It provides a virtual IP for reaching a Service from within the cluster.

questions.question: A container repeatedly exits, and the Pod shows CrashLoopBackOff. What does this indicate?
options: Kubernetes is delaying repeated container restart attempts
A readiness probe removed the Pod from service traffic
The Pod cannot find a suitable node
The image cannot be downloaded
questions.explanation: CrashLoopBackOff means the container keeps failing and Kubernetes backs off between restart attempts. Check its logs and termination details to find the underlying cause.

questions.question: Which command shows logs from the previous instance of a restarted container?
options: kubectl logs <pod> --history
kubectl logs <pod> --previous
kubectl get events <pod> --previous
kubectl describe <pod> --logs
questions.explanation: Use kubectl logs <pod> --previous to inspect the previous terminated container instance, if available. Add -c <container> for the relevant container in a multi-container Pod.

questions.question: What happens when a container’s readiness probe fails?
options: Kubernetes deletes the Pod
Kubernetes moves the Pod to another node
The Pod is marked unready and normally stops receiving matching Service traffic
Kubernetes immediately restarts the container
questions.explanation: Readiness controls whether the Pod is ready to receive traffic. A failed readiness probe does not itself restart a container; liveness probes can trigger restarts.

questions.question: A Pod requests 2 CPUs, but no eligible node has enough CPU available for scheduling. What normally happens?
options: An arbitrary running Pod is immediately evicted
The Pod remains Pending
The Pod starts with a CPU limit of 1
Kubernetes automatically lowers the request
questions.explanation: The scheduler uses resource requests when placing Pods. Without a suitable node, the Pod remains Pending. Check kubectl describe pod for scheduling events.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a StatefulSet?
options: Run one Pod on every eligible node
Expose applications outside the cluster
Run short-lived tasks until completion
Manage Pods with stable identities and persistent storage associations
questions.explanation: StatefulSets provide stable Pod identities and can associate each Pod with its own persistent volume claim. DaemonSets handle per-node workloads; Jobs handle run-to-completion tasks.

questions.question: A Service does not reach your application Pods. Which check directly verifies whether it selects those Pods?
options: Check that the Pods use the latest image tag
Compare the Service name with the Deployment name
Compare their creation timestamps
Compare the Service selector with the Pods’ labels
questions.explanation: A selector-based Service matches Pods by labels in its namespace. Also inspect EndpointSlices, Pod readiness, targetPort, and network policies when troubleshooting traffic.

questions.question: What does a namespace-scoped RoleBinding referencing a ClusterRole do?
options: Grants applicable permissions within the RoleBinding’s namespace
Grants access only to cluster-scoped resources
Converts the ClusterRole into a Role
Grants permissions across every namespace
questions.explanation: A RoleBinding limits its grant to its namespace, even when referencing a reusable ClusterRole. Cluster-wide grants require a ClusterRoleBinding.

questions.question: Which statement about Kubernetes Secrets is correct?
options: Secrets are always encrypted in etcd by default
Every Pod can read every Secret by default
Base64 encoding encrypts Secret values
Base64 alone provides no confidentiality; encryption at rest must be configured separately
questions.explanation: Base64 is encoding, not encryption. Configure encryption at rest and restrict access with RBAC. Managed Kubernetes providers may configure encryption for you.

questions.question: Why add a startup probe to a container that can take several minutes to initialize?
options: It reserves a node exclusively for the Pod
It increases the container memory limit
It prevents the container from ever restarting
It delays liveness and readiness probes until startup succeeds
questions.explanation: Startup probes give slow applications time to initialize. Once startup succeeds, normal readiness and liveness checks take over.

questions.question: What does this liveness configuration do after the application has started?
options: Marks the node permanently unschedulable
Scales the application to three replicas
Restarts the container after three consecutive failed checks
Deletes the Deployment after one failed check
questions.explanation: Liveness failure triggers a container restart after the configured failure threshold. Readiness controls traffic eligibility instead.
questions.code:
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: 8080
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 3

questions.question: How much CPU does this container request?
options: One quarter of a CPU
2.5 CPU cores
250 CPU cores
A quarter of the node’s total CPU capacity
questions.explanation: 1000m equals one CPU. CPU requests are absolute CPU quantities, not percentages of the node.

questions.question: A container exceeds its memory limit and its last termination reason is OOMKilled. What is the likely cause?
options: The image registry rejected the container
The container was terminated after exceeding its enforced memory allowance
The readiness probe redirected its memory
CPU throttling always produces this reason
questions.explanation: Memory limits can result in out-of-memory termination. Inspect usage, application behavior, limits, and termination details before increasing resources.

questions.question: A node has low measured CPU usage, yet a CPU-heavy Pod cannot be scheduled there. What should you inspect first?
options: The number of Dockerfiles in the repository
CPU already allocated through other Pods’ requests
Whether the Service uses port 80
The lexical order of Pod names
questions.explanation: Scheduling considers requested resources and placement constraints. Low instantaneous utilization does not mean unallocated requested capacity is available.

questions.question: For a healthy Deployment with four desired replicas, what does this strategy permit during an update?
options: Five unavailable replicas at once
At most three available replicas
Up to five replicas, while keeping at least four available
Exactly four replicas with up to one unavailable
questions.explanation: maxSurge permits one extra Pod; maxUnavailable zero prevents deliberately reducing available replicas below the desired count during rollout.
questions.code:
replicas: 4
strategy:
  type: RollingUpdate
  rollingUpdate:
    maxSurge: 1
    maxUnavailable: 0

questions.question: A Pod is waiting with ImagePullBackOff. Which investigation is most relevant?
options: Delete the application Service
Check the image name, registry access, credentials, and Pod events
Change the container’s working directory
Increase the readiness probe timeout only
questions.explanation: ImagePullBackOff indicates repeated image-pull failures with retry backoff. Events often identify missing tags, authentication failures, or registry connectivity problems.

questions.question: A regular init container exits with a nonzero status before application containers start. What normally happens in a Pod with restartPolicy Always?
options: The application containers start immediately anyway
The Service automatically repairs the init script
Kubernetes retries the init container before starting the application containers
The Pod skips all remaining init containers
questions.explanation: Regular init containers must complete successfully in sequence. Failures block application startup and are retried according to Pod behavior.

questions.question: You need a log-collection agent on each eligible node. Which workload controller fits best?
options: Job
StatefulSet
DaemonSet
CronJob
questions.explanation: A DaemonSet manages node-local Pods across eligible nodes. Node selectors, affinity, and tolerations can affect which nodes receive an agent.

questions.question: Which controller tracks a task that should run to successful completion?
options: Deployment
DaemonSet
Service
Job
questions.explanation: Jobs track successful completions and can retry failed work. Applications that must run continuously are usually managed by other workload controllers.

questions.question: A previous Job from this CronJob is still running when the next schedule arrives. What does Forbid do?
options: Skips creating an overlapping Job for that scheduled run
Queues an unlimited number of overlapping Jobs
Terminates the running Job immediately
Disables all future scheduling permanently
questions.explanation: Forbid prevents overlap among Jobs created by this same CronJob. It does not coordinate unrelated CronJobs.

questions.question: A client connects to this Service on port 80. Which Pod port receives the traffic?
options: The Pod’s first declared containerPort regardless of targetPort
questions.explanation: Service port is the client-facing port; targetPort identifies the destination port on selected Pods.

questions.question: A selector-based Service has no ready endpoints. Which condition could explain it?
options: The Pods have more than one label
The Service name differs from the Deployment name
Matching Pods are failing their readiness checks
The Deployment has a revision history limit
questions.explanation: Ready endpoints depend on matching, ready Pods under normal Service behavior. Check selectors, EndpointSlices, and Pod readiness together.

questions.question: From a Pod in namespace frontend, which name identifies Service api in namespace backend using normal Kubernetes DNS conventions?
options: api.backend.svc.cluster.local, assuming cluster.local is the cluster domain
Only the bare name api can cross namespaces
backend.api.frontend
api.frontend.svc.cluster.local
questions.explanation: Cross-namespace lookups include the Service namespace. The cluster DNS suffix can be configured, so cluster.local is an assumption here.

questions.question: You created an Ingress object, but no component handles incoming HTTP traffic. What is usually also required?
options: An Ingress controller implementing the selected ingress class
A ConfigMap with the same name as every Service
A StatefulSet named ingress
A Secret for every Pod even for plain HTTP
questions.explanation: An Ingress object declares routing rules; a controller implements them. Creating the API object alone does not deploy the controller.

questions.question: Two ingress NetworkPolicies select the same Pod. One allows port 80; the other allows port 443. With policy enforcement enabled, how are these permissions combined?
options: The second policy always overrides the first
The allowed ingress traffic is the union of both policies
Only the policy with the longest name applies
All ingress is denied because the rules conflict
questions.explanation: NetworkPolicy allows are additive. Multiple policies selecting a Pod contribute allowed traffic rather than overriding each other.

questions.question: After enabling default-deny egress, a Pod cannot resolve Service names. Which allowance may be missing?
options: Ingress from the container image registry
A larger Service targetPort
Egress to the cluster DNS service on the required DNS ports
A label named dns=true on the Deployment
questions.explanation: DNS lookups require network access to the cluster DNS implementation. Review UDP and TCP port 53 and the relevant destination selectors.

questions.question: A ConfigMap value is consumed through an environment variable. After updating the ConfigMap, how does an already-running container receive the new value?
options: kubectl get configmap rewrites its environment
The Service injects the value on each request
It generally needs to be restarted or replaced
The process environment updates automatically every second
questions.explanation: Environment variables are set when the container starts. Mounted ConfigMap files have different update behavior from environment variables.

questions.question: Will changes to this ConfigMap automatically update the mounted subPath file in an already-running container?
options: Yes, but only if the Service is NodePort
Yes, when kubectl logs is run
Yes, on every file read
No; ConfigMap subPath mounts do not receive automatic updates
questions.explanation: A ConfigMap mounted using subPath does not receive the automatic projected-volume updates. Recreate the container or change the mounting approach.
questions.code:
volumeMounts:
  - name: config
    mountPath: /app/settings.yaml
    subPath: settings.yaml

questions.question: A PersistentVolumeClaim remains Pending. What is a useful first investigation?
options: Rename the Service to match the claim
Inspect claim events, StorageClass provisioning, capacity, and access-mode compatibility
Restart CoreDNS before checking events
Increase the container CPU limit
questions.explanation: Binding and provisioning failures are usually visible in PVC events. StorageClass configuration and matching volume requirements are central checks.

questions.question: What does ReadWriteOnce mean for a PersistentVolume access mode?
options: Exactly one Pod may use the volume under all circumstances
Read-write mounting by a single node
The volume becomes read-only after the first write
Exactly one process may open a file
questions.explanation: ReadWriteOnce constrains node-level read-write mounting, not necessarily one Pod. ReadWriteOncePod is the distinct single-Pod access mode.

questions.question: A bound PV has reclaimPolicy Retain. What should you expect after its PVC is deleted?
options: The volume and data require manual reclamation rather than automatic deletion
The volume becomes a ConfigMap
The PV is automatically attached to every new PVC
The backing storage is always erased immediately
questions.explanation: Retain preserves the storage asset for administrator handling. It does not automatically make previously used storage safe for another claim.

questions.question: What does a toleration matching a NoSchedule taint guarantee?
options: The Pod can never be evicted
The Pod bypasses CPU and memory requests
The Pod must be placed on that node
Only that the matching taint will not block scheduling; other constraints still apply
questions.explanation: Tolerations permit placement despite matching taints. They do not select nodes or override resource and affinity constraints.

questions.question: What does this node selector require?
options: The Pod must run on a node labeled disktype=ssd
The Pod requests an SSD through a PVC automatically
The condition is only a soft preference
The scheduler adds that label to any chosen node
questions.explanation: nodeSelector is a hard label match for scheduling. If no eligible node matches, the Pod remains unscheduled.

questions.question: You want replicas of the same application placed on different nodes. Which feature directly expresses that relationship?
options: A Service sessionAffinity setting
A ConfigMap with one key per replica
A larger imagePullPolicy
Pod anti-affinity using a hostname topology key
questions.explanation: Pod anti-affinity can separate Pods based on labels and topology. Required rules can make Pods unschedulable when insufficient topology domains exist.

questions.question: How does kubectl cordon differ from kubectl drain?
options: Cordon blocks new scheduling; drain also attempts to evict eligible existing Pods
Drain only updates the node’s CPU requests
They both immediately power off the node
Cordon deletes all Pods; drain only changes node labels
questions.explanation: Cordon marks a node unschedulable. Drain performs maintenance-oriented eviction and respects relevant constraints such as disruption budgets.

questions.question: Three replicas are healthy. With this disruption budget, how many can normally be voluntarily evicted at once while maintaining the budget?
options: Three
Zero
One
Two
questions.explanation: With three healthy selected Pods and minAvailable two, one disruption is allowed. A PDB does not prevent all involuntary failures.
questions.code:
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: checkout

questions.question: An RBAC rule allows get on pods but not list. Which operation can still be denied?
options: Getting a named Pod when authorized in the namespace
Reading the API server version anonymously if allowed
Using the singular API resource name in documentation
Listing all Pods with kubectl get pods
questions.explanation: RBAC distinguishes get, list, and watch. Permission to retrieve one named object does not imply permission to list a collection.

questions.question: What identity does a Pod normally use for Kubernetes API authentication when a ServiceAccount token is mounted?
options: The ServiceAccount of the default namespace regardless of Pod namespace
The user who authored its Dockerfile
The Deployment name as a cluster administrator
The ServiceAccount assigned to that Pod in its namespace
questions.explanation: ServiceAccounts are namespaced identities for workloads. Their API permissions are controlled by RBAC grants rather than by the container image author.

questions.question: What is the purpose of this setting?
options: Grant the container root privileges on the host
Require the container to run as a non-root user
Make the image filesystem writable by all users
Automatically create an OS user in the image
questions.explanation: runAsNonRoot enforces a non-root execution requirement. It does not create users inside the image, and incompatible image settings can prevent startup.

questions.question: An app must write temporary files while using readOnlyRootFilesystem: true. What is an appropriate design?
options: Add a label named writable=true
Use a Service of type LoadBalancer
Disable all liveness probes
Mount a writable volume at the required temporary directory
questions.explanation: A read-only root filesystem can be combined with writable volumes at specific paths, such as an emptyDir mounted at /tmp.

questions.question: What happens if a container ignores graceful termination and remains running after its termination grace period expires?
options: The Service becomes permanently unavailable
Its remaining processes can be forcibly killed
The Pod automatically gains an unlimited grace period
The Deployment is deleted to preserve the container
questions.explanation: Kubernetes gives the container time to terminate gracefully, then can force termination. Applications should handle shutdown signals and stop accepting work appropriately.

questions.question: For CPU utilization-based HPA, a container uses 200m CPU and requests 500m. What is its CPU utilization relative to its request?
questions.explanation: CPU utilization for this HPA metric is usage divided by request. Requests are therefore important inputs to utilization-based scaling.

questions.question: A new Pod is rejected because the namespace has exhausted its CPU request quota. Which resource enforces that aggregate namespace limit?
options: LimitRange alone
ResourceQuota
EndpointSlice
PodDisruptionBudget
questions.explanation: ResourceQuota can bound aggregate namespace consumption. LimitRange typically supplies defaults or constrains individual objects within the namespace.

questions.question: Which object can set default container resource requests and limits for newly admitted Pods in a namespace?
options: LimitRange
VolumeAttachment
IngressClass
ServiceAccount
questions.explanation: A LimitRange can supply resource defaults and enforce minimums or maximums. Defaults apply during admission rather than retroactively changing running containers.

questions.question: A running application image has no shell or network tools. What can help inspect its Pod without rebuilding the application image?
options: An ephemeral debug container, subject to permissions and runtime support
Changing the Service to ExternalName
Adding commands to the Pod’s labels
Increasing revisionHistoryLimit
questions.explanation: kubectl debug can add an ephemeral container with diagnostic tools. Security policy and permissions still apply.

questions.question: What does the -c option select in this command?
options: The namespace named api
A ConfigMap named api
The container named api inside the Pod
A cluster context named api
questions.explanation: For multi-container Pods, -c chooses which container receives the exec request. The command after -- runs inside that container.

questions.question: Which Pods does this command select?
options: Pods having either label but not necessarily both
All Pods in namespaces named web or frontend
Pods having both app=web and tier=frontend
Only Pods whose names contain frontend
questions.explanation: Comma-separated equality requirements in this selector are combined with logical AND.

questions.question: A Deployment rollout introduced a broken image. What does kubectl rollout undo deployment/web normally do?
options: Rolls back to a previous retained Pod-template revision
Reverts all ConfigMaps in the namespace
Restores application database contents from backup
Reverts the Git commit that built the image
questions.explanation: Deployment rollback targets retained rollout history for the Pod template. It does not roll back external data or independently changed resources.

questions.question: Why should two unrelated Deployment controllers avoid overlapping Pod selectors?
options: They can interfere with management of matching workloads
Overlapping selectors automatically merge Deployments
Kubernetes converts their Pods into a StatefulSet
Selectors determine the order of container logs
questions.explanation: Controllers use selectors to identify their managed workload sets. Unintended overlap makes ownership and reconciliation behavior unsafe or confusing.
